title: Ministries
tomorrow: why did Jesus stand up to read, then sit down to talk?

segments.voice: Last week ended with the minutes on either side of Mass: a regular seat, arriving early, staying after. The line was early and staying.

Count the people up front at a Sunday Mass who aren't the priest: someone reading, servers in robes, a choir, people holding the cups at Communion. Where did they all come from? The answer starts with a complaint. In the Acts of the Apostles, the young church in Jerusalem is growing fast, and food is handed out daily to widows. Then the Greek-speaking believers begin to murmur: our widows are being overlooked. The apostles are stretched thin. So they call the whole community together, and they say…
screen: `WHO ARE ALL THESE PEOPLE?` → `OUR WIDOWS ARE OVERLOOKED.` → `THE APOSTLES CALL EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: …it isn't right for us to leave the word of God and serve tables. Choose from among you seven men of good reputation, full of the Spirit and wisdom, and we'll put them over this work. The whole crowd likes the plan. They choose Stephen and six others, and the apostles pray and lay hands on them. Tradition sees in these seven the first deacons. Notice how ministry is born here: from a need someone noticed, and from people willing to say, I can do that. Paul gives it a picture in his first letter to the Corinthians, one body with many members: "Now there are diversities of graces, but the same Spirit." The eye can't say to the hand, I don't need you. That's the room on Sunday. Readers who lend their voice, servers at the altar, a choir, ministers of Communion, visitors who carry Communion to the sick, catechists who teach. One to tell a friend: the Second Vatican Council taught that lay people share in Christ's mission through their baptism, not through a job title. On that teaching, everyone serves. A ministry just gives the serving a shape.
screen: `WE CAN'T LEAVE THE WORD TO SERVE TABLES.` · `CHOOSE SEVEN.` · `ONE BODY, MANY MEMBERS.` · `SERVICE FROM BAPTISM.` · then, large: `EVERYONE SERVES.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and paper and write one thing you're good at, plainly, the way you'd tell a friend: I can cook, I can fix bikes, I'm good with little kids, I can carry a tune. Under it, write one place it could serve, in a parish or anywhere people gather. If you pray, you can offer that line to God just as it is.
Ministries. The shapes that service takes in a parish, each one born from a need and a person willing to meet it. Today's word.
Carry this: everyone serves, from the first seven at the tables to whoever reads on Sunday. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Parishes have lay readers (lectors), altar servers, choirs, extraordinary ministers of Holy Communion, visitors to the sick and catechists, alongside the priest and deacon.

chat.meaning: In Acts, ministry began from a need and willing people, and Paul says one body, many members. Everyone serves; a ministry gives it a shape.

Acts of the Apostles.meaning: Luke's book about the early Church after Jesus

Stephen.meaning: one of the seven chosen to serve in Acts 6

Corinthians.meaning: the church in Corinth, to whom Paul wrote letters

catechists.meaning: people who teach the faith to others

Second Vatican Council.meaning: a council of the world's Catholic bishops held in Rome

notes: 1 Corinthians 12:4 quoted from Douay-Rheims; confirm exact wording. 12:21 ('the eye cannot say to the hand: I need not thy help') paraphrased.

Acts 6:1–6 paraphrased (Grecians murmuring against the Hebrews; widows neglected in the daily ministration; 'It is not reason that we should leave the word of God, and serve tables'; seven men of good reputation, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom; Stephen and six others named; prayer and laying on of hands). 'Seven' is the text's number. Confirm.
'Tradition sees in these seven the first deacons': the text does not call them deacons; hedged. Confirm framing.
Lumen Gentium 31, 33 and Apostolicam Actuositatem 2–3 paraphrased: the laity share in Christ's mission through baptism. Confirm.
